title: Tilt Decision
primary_metric: weighted effective kWh generated per panel per year, each month's modeled output weighted by the utility's time-of-use summer rate multiplier

options.A: Recommend Latitude Lock — fixed tilt angle equal to the site's latitude, maximizing total annual energy collected
options.B: Recommend Summer Shift — a shallower fixed tilt angle favoring the utility's highest-rate summer months

reinforcement_note: This case is a deliberate second, independent touch on Pre-Calculus/Trigonometric Functions, not a fresh gap-closer. tide-window is the group's first case and already carries new_coverage for all 11 group skills (radian, unit circle, sine/cosine/tangent function, amplitude, period-of-a-function, reference angle, and the three how-to bridges); every skill this case's deliverables (D1-D4) genuinely force -- degree/radian conversion, unit-circle sine/cosine/tangent evaluation, reference angles, amplitude/period identification -- already shows n>=1 in standards_spine.json, all credited to tide-window. Checked the group's remaining, still-uncovered-by-THIS-case skills before concluding there was nothing left to honestly claim: pythagorean-identity, inverse-trigonometric-function, how-to-verify-a-trigonometric-identity, how-to-solve-a-trigonometric-equation-over-a-given-interval, and how-to-evaluate-an-inverse-trigonometric-function are all n=1 (covered by deluge-gun, not this case), and none of them are skills this case's deliverables force -- D1-D4 never solve a trig equation, verify an identity, or evaluate an inverse trig function; they only convert angles and evaluate sine/cosine/tangent directly from the unit circle. So there is no adjacent uncovered skill this case's real math reaches. The pedagogical reason this case still exists despite the redundancy: the weekly assignment rotation needs more than one case per skill group so a single case being pulled, re-run, or found stale does not leave the group with zero live assignments -- Summer Shift vs. Latitude Lock is a genuinely different scenario and dataset (rate-weighted solar siting vs. tide-window's original context) that gives cohorts a second, independent problem to work the same skills against.

sources.claim: Representative site coordinates for a Sacramento, CA rooftop installation (Sacramento City Hall, used as the case's stated site point) and the derived Latitude Lock tilt angle (latitude rounded to nearest degree)
sources.title: Sacramento City Hall, 915, I Street, Downtown, Sacramento, Sacramento County, California, 95814, USA
sources.note: Used as a representative point for 'a residential rooftop in Sacramento,' not a verified specific street address. Latitude Lock's 39-degree tilt is derived from this latitude, rounded to the nearest whole degree. Data-decay re-check 2026-08-31: the live page now returns 38.582301, -121.49332 (a ~0.0007-degree/~90m drift from the value recorded here at original access). Immaterial to the case: the corrected latitude still rounds to a 39-degree tilt, and PVWatts/NOAA output at this displacement is unchanged to the precision this case uses. Not re-derived for this reason; flagged per case-readiness P6 rather than silently accepted.

sources.title: Optimum fixed orientations and benefits of tracking for capturing solar radiation in the continental United States (Solar Energy, 2011)
sources.note: General nationwide seasonal-tilt rule of thumb from a peer-reviewed study, not a Sacramento-specific design table. Summer Shift's 24-degree tilt = 38.5816 - 15 = 23.58, rounded to the nearest whole degree.

sources.claim: Modeled monthly and annual AC output per panel (0.4 kW / one 400W panel) at Option A's 39-degree tilt and Option B's 24-degree tilt, fixed rooftop array, azimuth 180 (true south), standard module type, 14% system losses
sources.title: PVWatts Calculator, v8 API
sources.note: Live API call at lat 38.5816, lon -121.4944, system_capacity=0.4, azimuth=180, tilt=39 (Option A) and tilt=24 (Option B), array_type=1 (fixed roof mount), module_type=0 (standard), losses=14 (PVWatts default). Weather source: NSRDB PSM V3 GOES TMY, station 131636 (Sacramento area). Every other input held identical between the two runs so the two columns differ only in tilt angle, per the case's Appendix B note. Data-decay re-check 2026-08-31: the developer.nlr.gov domain initially read as a possible typosquat of developer.nrel.gov (old domain now fails DNS resolution entirely). Independently verified as legitimate, not a spoof: the U.S. Department of Energy renamed NREL to the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) effective 2025-12-01, confirmed via energy.gov's own announcement (https://www.energy.gov/cmei/articles/energy-department-renames-nrel-national-lab-rockies) and DOE's OpenEI wiki (https://openei.org/wiki/National_Laboratory_of_the_Rockies), independent of the cited page's own self-description. The PVWatts v8 API and its underlying model are unchanged by the rename; the cited figures still resolve at the new domain.

sources.claim: SMUD residential Time-of-Day (5-8pm) rate schedule: summer season definition, on-peak hour window, summer on-peak rate, and non-summer off-peak rate
sources.value: Summer Jun1-Sep30; on-peak 5-8pm; summer on-peak $0.3765/kWh; non-summer off-peak $0.1285/kWh
sources.title: Time-of-Day (5-8pm) Rate — Rate details
sources.note: Utility's own published rate page, 2026 rates. The same non-summer season also carries its own 5-8pm on-peak rate of $0.1776/kWh; this case uses the off-peak rate ($0.1285) as 'the' non-summer rate since it is what most non-summer hours are billed at, matching the case's simplified month-level weighting (Appendix C row, Background). Multiplier = 0.3765/0.1285 = 2.93 (derived). Using the non-summer on-peak rate instead gives a multiplier of 2.12 — confirmed by re-running the D4 weighting under both interpretations: the weighted-output ranking between Option A and Option B is unchanged either way, only the margin size changes (2.13% vs 1.37%).

sources.claim: Solar elevation and azimuth angles at the site's latitude: four representative dates (2026 solstices/equinoxes, morning/solar-noon/afternoon) and twelve mid-month solar-noon samples
sources.units: degrees (elevation above horizon; azimuth clockwise from true north)
sources.title: Solar Calculator solar-position equations (solareqns.PDF)
sources.note: NOAA's interactive Solar Calculator is not a scriptable data source, so values were computed programmatically by implementing NOAA's own published solar-position algorithm (solar declination, equation of time, hour angle, elevation, azimuth) for lat 38.5816/lon -121.4944, calendar year 2026, Pacific time with correct PDT/PST offsets. Cross-checked against the closed-form identity solar-noon elevation = 90 - |latitude - declination|, which the computed solar-noon values reproduce exactly (e.g. summer solstice: 90 - (38.5816 - 23.44) = 74.86, matching the computed 74.9).

deliverables.text: A degrees-to-radians conversion table for the sun's solar-noon elevation angle at the site's latitude on each representative date in Appendix D, with every value shown in both degrees and radians and the conversion arithmetic shown for at least one entry.

A solar-position table for each representative date in Appendix D covering a morning, solar-noon, and afternoon sun position: each published sun azimuth-and-elevation pair converted into a standard-position angle, its reference angle identified and labeled, and the sine, cosine, and tangent of that angle found using the unit circle, with the full unit-circle reasoning shown for at least one entry from each quadrant encountered.

A single graph, spanning the full year, of the sun's solar-noon elevation angle as a sinusoidal function of the date, with the model's amplitude and period both identified, labeled directly on the graph, and computed from the data in Appendix D, with Latitude Lock's and Summer Shift's fixed tilt angles both drawn on the same graph as horizontal reference lines for comparison.

A monthly angle-of-incidence and relative-efficiency table for each tilt option, using the cosine relationship between each month's solar-noon elevation angle (from D2/D3) and the option's fixed tilt angle, checked for consistency against the modeled monthly output in Appendix B for at least two representative months — followed by a weighted-annual-output comparison table that carries that check forward, applying Appendix C's time-of-use rate multiplier month by month and summing into a single weighted effective annual kWh-per-panel figure for each option.

appendices.title: Modeled Monthly Output by Tilt Angle

balance.argument_a: Latitude Lock is the classically optimal fixed tilt for total annual energy collection: setting tilt equal to the site's 38.5816-degree latitude (rounded to 39 degrees) minimizes the sun's average angle of incidence integrated across the full year, so it wins on raw annual kWh per panel, 659.3 vs. 656.2 for Summer Shift's 24-degree tilt — a 0.47% edge, and the number a competing installer's quote is likely to print without qualification.
balance.argument_b: Summer Shift trades winter and shoulder-season output (already paid at the utility's cheaper non-summer rate) for a better angle match during the exact 4 months (June-September) the time-of-use schedule charges its 2.93x summer on-peak multiplier ($0.3765 vs. $0.1285 per kWh) — so its raw annual kWh trails Latitude Lock by 0.47%, yet once that multiplier is applied to Appendix B's monthly output curve, its rate-weighted effective annual kWh comes out ahead, 1187.5 vs. 1162.8, a 2.13% margin.
balance.margin_basis: Once Appendix B's PVWatts monthly output for both tilt angles and Appendix C's summer on-peak rate multiplier and summer-month definition are sourced, compute each option's weighted effective annual kWh per panel by multiplying every month's modeled output by that month's applicable rate multiplier (summer on-peak multiplier for summer months, 1.0 for non-summer months) and summing across the year; compare the two totals for A and B.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Number of panels in the Reyes household's array
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public record exists for a fictional household's specific array size. 20 panels of the named 400W module sizes to an 8.0 kW DC array, in range for a typical mid-size residential system in the Sacramento market.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: None. The case's primary metric is stated per panel, and panel count is identical for both options -- it cancels out of the comparison entirely and cannot flip the recommendation.

derived.note: raw_* = sum of Appendix B's twelve monthly per-panel kWh figures, no rate weighting. weighted_* = each month's Appendix B output multiplied by Appendix C's summer on-peak multiplier (2.93, summer months) or 1.0 (non-summer months), summed across the year -- this is the case's stated primary_metric. The *_alt row re-runs the same weighting using the non-summer ON-peak rate ($0.1776) instead of the off-peak rate ($0.1285) as the denominator (S6's documented alternate reading) -- Summer Shift still wins, only the margin narrows. See RESEARCH_LOG.md and cases/the-tilt-decision/sensitivity_model.py.

cohort_bands.note: The size this T2 case is authored for. Socratic plan and anchor timings run as written; both stand/sit votes are taken as a group; the twist (off-peak vs. on-peak non-summer rate) drops at the same relative point and both deep-conflict threads run.

Anchors 2-3 combine into one pass; the deep-conflict thread runs as a single combined thread (raw-vs-weighted framing folded into the rate-convention thread) instead of the full three; total runtime shortens proportionally.

No vote to take -- Anchor 1 becomes a stated initial position instead of a stand/sit count; the guide plays devil's advocate directly rather than cold-calling; Socratic question 2 (the break-even multiplier) still lands but is asked directly rather than opened to the room.

sensitivity_note: Margin (~2.13%) is fairly tight and is sensitive to which SMUD non-summer rate is used as the multiplier's denominator (off-peak $0.1285 -> 2.93x -> 2.13% margin; on-peak $0.1776 -> 2.12x -> 1.37% margin). Summer Shift wins the weighted metric under both interpretations; only the margin size changes, not the winner. Also sensitive to the exact tilt angles chosen for Option A/B within the racking's 10-60 degree range.
